summary: This RFC defines RADIUS attributes for Proxy Mobile IPv6. The mobile access gateway and local mobility anchor use RADIUS interfaces with the AAA server for authentication, authorization, and policy.

eli5.summary: Mobile helpers need to ask a central office if someone is allowed in, and under what rules. This adds the fields for that to RADIUS.

questions: what is radius support for proxy mobile ipv6
what is the mip6 feature vector
what does the mag send to the aaa server
subtitle: New RADIUS attributes that let Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateways fetch a device's mobility settings and get a mobility session authorized.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 needs per-device policy (which anchor to use, which addresses to hand out) and an authorization check, but the RADIUS servers many networks already run had no standard way to carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 18 new RADIUS attributes, two new capability bits for MIP6-Feature-Vector, and rules for two interfaces: mobile access gateway to AAA server, and local mobility anchor to AAA server. It also sets a baseline for accounting.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use RADIUS for PMIPv6 session setup, address assignment and accounting in home, visited and mixed deployments. This is a Proposed Standard, and it has been updated by RFC 8044.

today: RFC 6572 is a Proposed Standard from June 2012 and has been updated by RFC 8044. It has not been obsoleted, per the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why PMIPv6 Needs RADIUS
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, from RFC 5213) gives a mobile node IP mobility without the node doing any mobility signaling itself. Two network elements do the work: the mobile access gateway (MAG), which detects the node's movement and starts the signaling, and the local mobility anchor (LMA), which the MAG signals to. Both use the AAA infrastructure to fetch the node's policy profile and to authorize the service.

RFC 6572 defines a RADIUS profile and the attributes for it. One interface runs between the MAG and the AAA server and carries the per-node policy profile from a remote policy store to the MAG. A second runs between the LMA and the AAA server and authorizes the PMIPv6 signaling the LMA receives. Both cases are covered where the node attaches from its home network and where it attaches from a visited network.

The document also defines terms it needs: the Network Access Server (NAS, assumed to be co-located with the MAG), the Home AAA (HAAA) server, the Visited AAA (VAAA) server that proxies requests to the HAAA, and the Local AAA (LAAA) proxy.
sections.eli5: Helpers at the doors need to ask the office what a visitor is allowed to do. RADIUS is the phone line they already have, so this RFC teaches it the new questions.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit Together
sections.content:
The node's policy profile sits in a policy store. The store can be co-located with the mobility agents or reached through RADIUS. When a node attaches, the NAS may run network access authentication, typically based on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), and query the HAAA. If it succeeds, the node's policy profile comes back in the RADIUS exchange. The profile should say clearly which address types the node gets, since a node may be IPv4-only, IPv6-only or dual-stack.

After that, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) to the LMA. On receiving it, the LMA asks the HAAA for the node's profile so it can authorize and activate the mobility service.

Three deployment models are supported, depending on where the MAG and LMA sit. In each case a VAAA, when present, acts as a proxy and may add information to HAAA replies to reflect local policy.
sections.eli5: First the door helper checks the visitor and learns the rules. Then the helper tells the room manager, and the room manager double-checks with the office before saying yes.

sections.title: The New Attributes
sections.content:
Section 4 defines the attributes. Most come in a Home and a Visited variant, used depending on which network the LMA is in. They fall into groups:

  • Identity and service: Mobile-Node-Identifier (145) carries the identifier to use in the PBU and PBA exchange, for cases where the access-authentication identity is hidden or differs. Service-Selection (146) names the service or external network. Calling-Station-Id (31) carries the node's link-layer identifier, and Chargeable-User-Identity (89) is a temporary billing handle.
  • LMA address: PMIP6-Home-LMA-IPv6-Address (147), PMIP6-Visited-LMA-IPv6-Address (148) and their IPv4 versions (149, 150).
  • Node addresses: home network prefix (151, 152), interface identifier (153, 154) and IPv4 home address (155, 156).
  • Helpers: DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 server addresses (157 to 160) for a MAG acting as a DHCP relay, and IPv4 default gateway (161, 162), which must belong to the subnet of the matching IPv4 home address attribute.

Where a prefix or address is delegated to the AAA server, the LMA sends an all-zero value (:: or 0.0.0.0) in the Access-Request, with the prefix length set to 128 or 32 respectively, and the server returns the assigned value. Interface identifiers SHOULD be chosen so that individual nodes cannot be tracked between sessions.
sections.eli5: The new form boxes say things like which room manager to use, what address to give the visitor, and which helper hands out addresses. Each box has a version for home and a version for away.

sections.title: The MAG to AAA Interface
sections.content:
The MAG uses RADIUS to fetch the policy profile when a node attaches. Depending on policy and network, it can receive configuration for the home or visited scenario, the address of the designated LMA, the IPv4 or IPv6 configuration for the node, and DHCP relay attributes.

The User-Name attribute MUST be present in the Access-Request and, if a node identity is available, MUST be a Network Access Identifier (NAI). At minimum the home realm must be known, otherwise the MAG cannot route the request to the right HAAA. If that identity is unsuitable for the later PBU and PBA messages, the HAAA MUST supply the identifier with Mobile-Node-Identifier, and the MAG MUST use it.

At least one of NAS-IP-Address, NAS-IPv6-Address or NAS-Identifier MUST be present. Service-Type SHOULD be 1 (Login), and NAS-Port-Type SHOULD be present. The section ends with a table of which attributes may appear in Request, Accept, Reject and Challenge messages.
sections.eli5: The door helper has to give the office a name and say which door they are at. If the visitor's real name should stay secret, the office can hand back a different name to use inside.

sections.title: The LMA to AAA Interface
sections.content:
The LMA-to-HAAA interface is used to authorize incoming PBUs, to tell the HAAA which LMA address was chosen, to delegate assignment of the home network prefix or IPv4 home address to the HAAA, and for accounting and session management.

The Access-Request SHOULD carry the node's identity in User-Name, strongly recommended to match the MN-Identifier in the PBU. Calling-Station-Id and Service-Selection SHOULD be included when the PBU carried the matching options. Service-Type MUST be 17 (Authorize Only). If authorization fails, the LMA rejects the PBU and MUST send back a PBA with an appropriate error status; the Access-Reject MAY include a Reply-Message giving the reason.

Authorization MUST be done at least for the initial PBU of a mobility session when this interface is deployed, and MAY be repeated for re-registrations and handovers. With dynamic LMA discovery (RFC 6097), the LMA address, its Fully Qualified Domain Name, or both are sent to the HAAA. Which entity manages addresses is deployment specific and MUST be agreed in advance.
sections.eli5: When the room manager gets a request, the manager checks with the office. If the answer is no, the manager tells the door helper why not.

sections.title: Accounting
sections.content:
RADIUS on the MAG and LMA also enables metering of the node's traffic, called accounting. Accounting follows RFC 2865 and RFC 2866. If accounting is turned on in the node's policy profile, local routing SHOULD NOT be enabled.

Both the LMA and the MAG interfaces MUST support transfer of accounting records. These records should include, but are not limited to, the time a binding cache entry was created and deleted and the number of octets the node sent and received over the bi-directional tunnel. If a MAG routes traffic locally between a visiting node and a locally attached correspondent node instead of using the reverse tunnel, that traffic MUST also be reported to the accounting servers.

A table lists the extra attributes that may appear in Accounting-Requests on top of those RFC 2866 and RFC 2869 already require.
sections.eli5: Like a turnstile counter, the helpers write down when each visitor came and left and how much they used, and send the tally to the office.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
RADIUS messages may travel between the MAG or LMA and the RADIUS server through one or more AAA brokers or proxies. In that case the communication relies on the security properties of those intermediaries.

For privacy, the considerations of the RADIUS base protocol (RFC 2865), RADIUS Accounting (RFC 2866) and the RADIUS EAP application (RFC 3579) apply. The MAG, LMA and AAA server SHOULD avoid including personally identifying information, such as a node's interface ID, link-layer address or NAI, except as needed, and SHOULD take special care if identity hiding is desired.
sections.eli5: Messages might pass through other offices on the way, so they should only carry the personal details that are truly needed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC defines 18 new RADIUS attribute type values, from Mobile-Node-Identifier (145) through PMIP6-Visited-IPv4-Gateway (162). It also adds two values to the Mobility Capability registry (from RFC 5447), used with the MIP6-Feature-Vector attribute: IP4_TRANSPORT_SUPPORTED (0x0000800000000000) and IP4_HOA_ONLY_SUPPORTED (0x0001000000000000).

The feature vector is a 64-bit flags field. PMIP6_SUPPORTED alone means only IPv6 mobility is authorized, with IP4_HOA_ONLY_SUPPORTED added means only IPv4, and with IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED added means both. A contradicting combination makes a client treat an Access-Accept as a reject, and makes a server answer an Access-Request with an Access-Reject; both SHOULD log it.
sections.eli5: The new boxes get official numbers in a public list so nobody picks the same number for something else.

messages.label: Access-Request
messages.note: Network access authentication and profile query.

messages.label: Access-Accept
messages.note: Carries the node's policy profile attributes.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: At least 4 and no larger than 20.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: Prefix-Length
fields.desc: Length of the home network prefix, 0 to 128; 128 if the prefix is ::.

fields.name: Home MN-HNP
fields.desc: The prefix, up to 16 octets; bits outside the Prefix-Length must be zero.

viz.caption: MIP6-FEATURE-VECTOR CAPABILITY BITS USED BY RFC 6572

items.label: IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED
items.desc: Used as defined in RFC 5779; IPv4 home address assignment is defined by RFC 5844.

items.label: IP4_TRANSPORT_SUPPORTED
items.desc: New. The MAG can use IPv4 encapsulation to the LMA; if unset in the reply, the AAA does not authorize it.

items.label: IP4_HOA_ONLY_SUPPORTED
items.desc: New. Only IPv4 mobility is authorized; PMIP6_SUPPORTED MUST be set and IP4_HOA_SUPPORTED MUST NOT.
